content: An advance health care directive, also known as a living will or will to live, is a legal document that outlines a person’s preferences for medical treatment in situations where they are unable to provide informed consent due to incapacity. This directive is often accompanied by a health care proxy or a specific type of power of attorney, which designates an individual to make health care decisions on behalf of the principal if they are unable to do so. These legal instruments are typically witnessed or notarized to ensure their validity. A living will generally includes specific instructions regarding the course of treatment to be followed by caregivers. In some cases, it may explicitly forbid certain treatments, including the provision of food and water, if the individual is incapacitated and unable to communicate their wishes. This is referred to as an individual health care instruction. On the other hand, a power of attorney for health care appoints a proxy to make health care decisions on behalf of the principal in such situations. The term will to live emphasizes the desire to prolong life as much as possible, contrasting with directives that focus on refusing treatment in severe medical conditions. Advance Health Care Directives in Specific Countries Australia In Australia, when patients aged 80 years or older are hospitalized, they are often presented with structured sessions led by trained non-medical facilitators to discuss their preferences for medical interventions. The outcomes of these discussions include: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): 56% chose not to receive CPR. 30% agreed to CPR only if the doctor anticipated a good outcome. 14% deferred the decision to the doctor or a surrogate. Life-prolonging treatment: 41% declined life-prolonging treatment. 39% agreed to it if the doctor anticipated a good outcome. 20% deferred the decision to the doctor or a surrogate. Netherlands In the Netherlands, individuals can specify the circumstances under which they would want euthanasia through a written euthanasia directive. This document helps establish the patient’s previously expressed wishes, even if they are no longer able to communicate. However, the directive is only one factor considered in the decision-making process. Two independent physicians must agree that the patient is terminally ill with no hope of recovery. Family members and organizations may also hold proxies to enforce such directives. Establishing these directives is relatively straightforward in the Netherlands. United States In the United States: When individuals engage in advanced care planning during the last two years of life, 96% prefer comfort care, while only 2% request all care possible. Advanced care planning increases the likelihood that terminal care aligns with the individual’s preferences. Despite its benefits, only 17% of claims submitted to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for patients aged 65 or older indicate advanced care planning. Most states recognize living wills or the designation of a health care proxy. However, a 2002 report by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation found that only seven states met the standards of the Uniform Rights of the Terminally Ill Act. Surveys reveal that one-third of Americans have had to make end-of-life care decisions for a loved one. Physicians may underestimate patients’ willingness to engage in discussions about advanced care planning and end-of-life care. Benefits of Advance Care Planning Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that the use of advance directives, including living wills and health care proxies, improves the alignment between end-of-life care choices and actions. In one trial, 81% of patients in the intervention group (encouraged to engage in advance care planning) completed advance care planning. Among those who died: 86% in the intervention group received terminal care matching their wishes, compared to 30% in the control group. Family members of patients in the intervention group reported significantly higher satisfaction and lower levels of stress, anxiety, and depression. Cohort studies using Medicare’s Health and Retirement Study (HRS) found that most individuals preferred comfort care (96%), while only 2% requested all care possible. Surrogates who were aware of their loved one’s wishes experienced less stress compared to those who made decisions without certainty about the patient’s preferences. A systematic review of observational studies highlighted that knowing which treatment aligns with the patient’s preferences reduces the negative impact on surrogates. Methods to Promote Advance Care Planning Advance care planning can be promoted through: Facilitated advance care planning for hospitalized patients. In-person guidance for homeless individuals provided by social workers using tools like the SELPH AD. Decision aids designed to guide patients and families in making informed choices. However, many of these aids are proprietary or not publicly available. The Physician’s Perspective A qualitative survey of internal medicine doctors in the United States identified three sources of satisfaction in medical practice: 1. Realizing a fundamental change in perspective through patient experiences. 2. Making a meaningful difference in someone’s life. 3. Building connections with patients. Meaningful events, such as connecting with patients during end-of-life care, often occur in situations that might otherwise be perceived as failures of medical care. Factors associated with a good death include: Effective pain and symptom management. Clear decision-making and communication with physicians. Preparation for death, including understanding what to expect and planning for post-death events. Completion, which involves resolving conflicts, spending time with loved ones, and saying goodbye. Contributing to others, such as imparting life lessons or ensuring loved ones are cared for. Affirmation of the whole person, where physicians engage with patients on a personal level, discussing their lives, families, and interests. End-of-Life Discussions End-of-life discussions are a critical component of the physician-patient relationship and are associated with improved quality of life for both patients and their families. Patients with strong religious coping mechanisms may be more inclined to pursue life-prolonging measures. Randomized controlled trials have shown that communication interventions, such as family conferences and informational brochures, can reduce the burden of bereavement for family members. Sedation and Withdrawal of Life Support Providing sedation at the end of life and withdrawing life support are challenging issues for physicians. Sequential withdrawal of life support components, rather than abrupt cessation, may improve the experience for surviving family members. Extubation of intubated patients before death is associated with greater satisfaction among families. In summary, advance care planning and end-of-life discussions are essential for aligning medical care with patient preferences, reducing stress for families, and ensuring a dignified and meaningful death.
